```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(distmer)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(kableExtra)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

Random effects describe ecological replication:  `(1 | site)` says that observations from the same site share a
site-level community component. Nested, blocked, and random-slope terms
extend that idea to more structured sampling.

- `(1 | site)` — repeated observations within sites; treatments assigned among
  sites are tested with sites as the independent units.
- `(1 | region/site)` — sites nested within regions; each predictor is tested
  at the hierarchy level where it varies.
- `(1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block)` — a treatment randomized within blocks;
  the declared treatment-by-block variation supplies the treatment denominator.
- `(1 | region/site) + (1 | treatment:region) + (1 | treatment:region:site)` — treatment crossed with a nested region/site
  hierarchy.
- `(1 + condition | subject)` or `(1 + x | group)` — correlated random
  intercepts and slopes for complete repeated units.

`distmer` deliberately borrows `lmer` formula notation because it is a familiar and concise
way to state this hierarchy. `distmer`applies the declared fixed and random subspaces to a Gower-centred
dissimilarity matrix and obtains inference from design-appropriate
denominators and restricted permutations.

### Simple random effects:

Herbivory on coral reefs has a strong impact on macrobenthic community succession. This can be
demonstrated by using tiles placed in herbivore exclusion cages, typically "open", "partial" and "caged" treatments
(see [Evensen et al 2021](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.3536) for details).

Below is changes in [community succession](https://github.com/nickevensen/Palau-benthic-community-succession/) through time using the open surfaces of tiles ("crowns") across different caging treatments:

```{r data, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=10, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(distmer)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)


coralsuccession <- read.csv("~/distmer/code/Macro_communities.csv") |>
  filter(Nutrients == "Normal") |>
  filter(Microhabitat == "Crown")

env <- coralsuccession[,1:5]
coral <- coralsuccession[,6:17]
coral_bray <- vegdist(decostand(coral, method = "hellinger"), method = "bray")

coral_pcoa <- cmdscale(coral_bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE, add = TRUE)

coral_pcoa_scores <- as.data.frame(coral_pcoa$points) |>
  setNames(c("PCoA1", "PCoA2")) |>
  bind_cols(env) |>
  group_by(Caging, Timepoint) |>
  summarise(PCoA1=mean(PCoA1), PCoA2=mean(PCoA2))

coral_scores <- wascores(coral_pcoa$points, coral) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column() |>
  setNames(c("Taxa", "PCoA1", "PCoA2"))


a <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
  geom_point(data = coral_pcoa_scores, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, fill=Caging), shape=21) +
  geom_text(data = coral_pcoa_scores, aes(PCoA1-0.01, PCoA2+0.01, label=Timepoint/7), size=2.5) +
  geom_path(data = coral_pcoa_scores, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, group=Caging),
            colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.02, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1),
        legend.key = element_blank()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = NULL))

b <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
  geom_segment(data = coral_scores, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PCoA1, yend = PCoA2),
      arrow = arrow( length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"),
      colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text_repel(data = coral_scores, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, label=Taxa), size=2)

a|b

```

There are 5 Timepoints, and 18 tiles in total (n=6 per treatment).

The correct structure to explore the effect of caging over time is `Caging * Timepoint + (1 | Tile)`, where Timepoint as a fixed within-tile factor whose effect (and its interaction with Caging) we want to test, while Tile is a random intercept absorbing tile-to-tile variation.

Using `distmer` with tile as a random effect, both `Timepoint` and `Caging` treatment have a significant effect on benthic community structure:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fm1 <- permanova(coral_bray ~ Caging + Timepoint + (1 | Tile), env, type="III", permutations=9999, seed=101)
fm1$table |> tab()
```
With (1|Tile) as a random effect, pseudo-F (4.89) is (correctly) tested against MS 0.191 (tile-level), not against MS 0.076 (residual) as under `adonis2()`. Testing it against the residual would have inflated the apparent significance, so the correct stratification (1|tile) is more conservative.

Exploring the pairwise contrasts, the `Caging` treatment operates exactly as expected: Open and Partial treatments show no difference, while Caged treatments differ from both Open and Partial:

```{r}
permanova_contrasts(fm1, type = "pairwise", factor="Caging") |> tab()
```

### Nested hierarchies with unequal effort

Ecological surveys are rarely balanced. `(1 | region/site/quadrat)` states the containment; `distmer` then
tests each fixed term at the level where it actually varies, and does not
require equal replication at any level.

The survey below has eight regions, two sites in each, and either three or two
quadrats per site depending on which survey round the region fell in. Reef
status is a property of the region; wave exposure varies between replicates
inside a quadrat.

```{r nested-survey, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2024)
quadrats_per_site <- c(3, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2)

survey <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:8, function(region) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(site) {
    do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(quadrats_per_site[region]), function(quadrat) {
      data.frame(region = paste0("R", region), site = paste0("S", site),
                 quadrat = paste0("Q", quadrat), replicate = 1:3)
    }))
  }))
}))

for (v in c("region", "site", "quadrat")) survey[[v]] <- factor(survey[[v]])
survey$status <- factor(
  ifelse(as.integer(survey$region) <= 4, "reference", "impacted"),
  levels = c("reference", "impacted")
)
survey$exposure <- factor(rep_len(c("sheltered", "exposed"), nrow(survey)))

region_effect <- rnorm(8, 0, 0.6)
latent <- 1.1 * (survey$status == "impacted") +
  0.7 * (survey$exposure == "exposed") +
  region_effect[as.integer(survey$region)] + rnorm(nrow(survey), 0, 0.5)
species <- sapply(1:12, function(k) {
  rpois(nrow(survey), lambda = exp(1.2 + 0.45 * k / 12 * latent))
})
colnames(species) <- paste0("sp", 1:12)
survey_bray <- vegdist(species, method = "bray")

fm_nested <- permanova(
  survey_bray ~ status + exposure + (1 | region / site / quadrat),
  survey, permutations = 999, seed = 11
)
fm_nested$table |> tab()
```

Each term found its own stratum. `status` is constant within a region, so it is
tested against variation among regions (6 df) with whole regions permuted.
`exposure` varies inside a quadrat, so it is tested against the residual (79 df)
with observations permuted within quadrats. Testing `status` against the
residual would treat 120 replicates as 120 independent units and badly overstate
the evidence.

Because effort is unequal, the question of *what* a region centroid means
matters. `distmer` averages upwards in stages: replicates onto quadrat
centroids, quadrat centroids onto their site with equal weight per quadrat, and
site centroids onto their region with equal weight per site. A region surveyed
with three quadrats per site therefore does not count for more than one surveyed
with two. Permutation respects the same structure: a region moves only among
regions whose whole sub-tree has the same shape, so the two survey rounds are
never exchanged with one another.

Any number of fixed terms is allowed, including interactions and continuous
covariates, and `type` selects the sums-of-squares partition among the terms
that share a level.

`distinct_statistics` and `minimum_attainable_p` are recorded on every test.
The level the warning is written against is the `distmer.resolution_alpha`
option, `0.05` by default; see `` ?`distmer-options` `` for that and the other
reporting options, none of which change an inferential result.

### Random slopes:

For a more complex example:

The `vegan::pyrifos` data contain aquatic-invertebrate communities from 12 ditches sampled repeatedly before and after insecticide application. Dose was assigned to ditches, so ditch is the experimental unit. Here four balanced post-treatment dates are used per ditch, where each trajectory is an individual ditch according to dose:

```{r repeated-ordination, fig.alt="Post-treatment Pyrifos samples connected through time within each ditch", fig.height=5, fig.width=5}

data(pyrifos, package = "vegan")
ditch <- gl(12, 1, length = nrow(pyrifos))
week <- rep(c(-4, -1, 0.1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 15, 19, 24), each = 12)
dose_by_ditch <- c(0.1, 0, 0, 0.9, 0, 44, 6, 0.1, 44, 0.9, 0, 6)
dose <- factor(rep(dose_by_ditch, 11))
keep <- week %in% c(1, 2, 4, 8)

community <- pyrifos[keep, ]
pyrifos_env <- data.frame(
  ditch = droplevels(ditch[keep]),
  dose = droplevels(dose[keep]),
  week = week[keep]
)
pyrifos_bray <- vegdist(community, method = "bray")

ditch_ord <- cmdscale(pyrifos_bray, k = 2)
ditch_ord <- cbind(
  pyrifos_env,
  data.frame(Axis1 = ditch_ord[, 1], Axis2 = ditch_ord[, 2])
)

ggplot() +
  geom_path(data = ditch_ord, aes(Axis1, Axis2, group = ditch, colour = dose, order = week), alpha = 0.65, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = ditch_ord, aes(Axis1, Axis2, group = ditch, fill = dose, order = week), shape=21, alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.8, 4), breaks = c(1, 4, 8)) +
  labs(x = "PCoA axis 1", y = "PCoA axis 2", colour = "Dose",
       size = "Week")

```

For a balanced two-condition comparison, an early (1-2 weeks) and late (>3 week) period is defined for each ditch (balanced with two
observations in each ditch-period cell).

Visualising the mean PCoA axis 1 within ditch and period indicates ditches need not share the same early-to-late change:

```{r period-plot, fig.alt="Early to late changes on PCoA axis 1 for each Pyrifos ditch", fig.height=5, fig.width=4}
period_env <- transform(
  pyrifos_env,
  period = factor(
    ifelse(week %in% c(1, 2), "early", "late"),
    levels = c("early", "late")
  )
)

period_ord <- transform(ditch_ord, period = period_env$period)
period_centres <- aggregate(
  cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ ditch + period,
  data = period_ord, FUN = mean
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = period_centres, aes(period, Axis1, group = ditch), colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = period_centres, aes(period, Axis1, group = ditch, fill = ditch), shape=21, size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Mean PCoA axis 1 within ditch and period")
```


Using a random intercept allows ditches to have different average communities, while a
random slope allows their within-ditch changes to differ.

```{r categorical-slope}
period_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ period + (1 + period | ditch),
  period_env, permutations = "all", seed = 26
)

summary(period_fit) |> tab()
```

A numeric gradient can also vary by unit. With four post-treatment weeks,
`(1 + week | ditch)` estimates one within-ditch community slope and tests the
equally weighted average slope against the variation among ditch slopes.

```{r continuous-slope}
continuous_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ week + (1 + week | ditch),
  pyrifos_env, permutations = 999, seed = 26
)

summary(continuous_fit) |> tab()

```
### Only random effects

`distmer` tests fixed effects against random strata, so a model with no fixed
term has nothing to test. `permanova()` refuses it rather than returning a sums
of squares table with no statistic, which would read like a result:

```{r random-only-error, error=TRUE}
permanova(pyrifos_bray ~ (1 | ditch), pyrifos_env)
```

The variance components themselves *are* available — they simply are not a
test. Call the estimator directly on the compiled design:

```{r random-only-components}
random_only <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ (1 | ditch), pyrifos_env, pyrifos_bray
)
estimate_variance_components(random_only)$unrestricted
```

For a `/`-generated hierarchy use `estimate_nested_variance_components()`,
which returns one component per level plus the residual and reproduces the
classical nested analysis-of-variance decomposition exactly.



### What distmer covers

`distmer` covers designs built on a single random structure — one grouping
factor, one containment chain of any depth, or one declared treatment-by-block
interaction — and, through `permanova_crossed_incomplete()`, designs whose
random terms are crossed rather than chained. Within either scope, imbalance is
allowed throughout, and cells may be missing entirely.

```{r scope-covered, echo=FALSE}
covered <- data.frame(
  Formula = c(
    "(1 | site)",
    "(1 | site) with several fixed factors",
    "(1 | region/site), (1 | region/site/quadrat), deeper",
    "(1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block)",
    "(1 | unit) + (1 | unit:subplot)",
    "(1 | region/site) + (1 | treatment:region) + (1 | treatment:region:site)",
    "(1 | a) + (1 | b), with or without (1 | a:b)",
    "(1 | t:unit) + (1 | t:unit:sub) + (1 | t:unit:time)",
    "numeric covariates alongside any of the above",
    "no random term at all, with empty cells",
    "(1 + condition | subject)",
    "(1 + x | group)"
  ),
  Design = c(
    "repeated observations within sites",
    "split-plot / randomized block, with or without covariates",
    "nested hierarchy of any depth",
    "treatment randomized within blocks",
    "asymmetric nested design, three error strata",
    "treatment crossed with a nested hierarchy",
    "two crossed random factors",
    "nested hierarchy crossed with a repeated measure",
    "covariate-adjusted designs",
    "incomplete fixed factorial",
    "complete two-condition repeated measures",
    "random slopes on a numeric covariate"
  ),
  `Tested against` = c(
    "among-site variation",
    "unit stratum or within-unit residual, per term",
    "the stratum where each term varies",
    "declared treatment-by-block variation",
    "unit, unit-by-subplot, and residual strata",
    "treatment-by-region interaction",
    "the stratum carrying the matching components",
    "the stratum each term varies over, by expected mean squares",
    "the residual, at one degree of freedom per slope",
    "the residual",
    "among-subject variation in the condition difference",
    "among-group variation in slopes"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kbl(covered) |> kable_styling(font_size = 12)
```

Unequal replication is supported at every level of a nesting chain, in
single-intercept designs, and in incomplete blocks. Empty cells reduce a term to
the dimension it can actually estimate rather than being refused, and
`nominal_df` records what a complete design would have given. The two
random-slope forms are the exception: both require complete, equally replicated
units.

Crossed random structures are handled by `permanova_crossed_incomplete()`, which
derives each denominator from the design's expected mean squares under the
restricted parameterisation, and reports a Freedman-Lane permutation p-value.
`hypothesis` selects Type I, II or III sums of squares; Type II is the default
because it stays well posed when cells are missing, where Type III can leave a
main effect spanned by a term containing it and report no estimable degrees of
freedom.

### What distmer doesn't cover (yet)

The remaining boundary is a random slope alongside anything else, and hierarchies
that branch.

```{r scope-uncovered, echo=FALSE}
uncovered <- data.frame(
  Formula = c(
    "(1 + x | g) with any other random term",
    "(1 | a/b) + (1 | c)",
    "(1 | a/b) + (1 | a/c)",
    "~ (1 | g) with no fixed term",
    "a factor that is both fixed and random",
    "(0 + x | g), (x | g), (1 + x || g)"
  ),
  Status = c(
    "refused",
    "refused: a chain crossed with an unrelated factor",
    "refused: branching hierarchies",
    "refused: there is nothing to test",
    "refused",
    "not accepted"
  ),
  Instead = c(
    "drop to a single random structure",
    "declare the validated hybrid form, or drop the crossed term",
    "one containment chain only",
    "estimate_variance_components(), or estimate_nested_variance_components()",
    "usually a misdeclared '/'; see the error text",
    "write (1 + x | g); uncorrelated slopes are unsupported"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kbl(uncovered) |> kable_styling(font_size = 12)
```

Correlation structures such as AR(1) or spatial covariance, and group-varying
residual variance, are outside the formula grammar entirely.

Refusals are deliberate. A formula that parses is not automatically a defensible
permutation design, and `distmer` declines a design rather than assign it a
denominator it cannot justify. `permanova_capabilities()` returns the same
contract in machine-readable form.



## Implementation

For exact detail, permanova() performs the following sequence:

1. It validates the dissimilarity and computes
   `G = -0.5 J D^2 J`. The same centring applies to every distance matrix;
   Euclidean distances give a positive semi-definite `G`, while signed axes
   from non-Euclidean distances remain in the analysis.
2. It converts fixed terms into estimable model subspaces and records whether
   each random term is a main grouping factor, a nesting declaration, an
   explicit interaction, or a random slope.
3. It checks balance, containment, crossing, cell completeness, confounding,
   and the level at which each predictor varies.
4. For supported balanced designs it derives the exact expected-mean-square
   (EMS) denominator. For supported unbalanced designs it works with equally
   weighted unit centroids or profiles and never invents an unbalanced EMS.
5. It constructs the permitted residual rearrangements, intact-unit
   permutations, or whole-unit sign flips, then reports the estimand,
   denominator, exchangeable unit, attainable permutations, and assumptions.

If no validated method matches the declared design, the model stops. A formula
that parses is not automatically a defensible permutation design.

Most users only need `permanova()`. The functions below are useful
for inspecting, validating, extending a particular design, or understanding how `distmer` works:

```{r implementation-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
implementation <- data.frame(
  `Formula pattern` = c(
    "d ~ a",
    "d ~ a + b (unbalanced, type = )",
    "d ~ a + (1 | site)",
    "d ~ a + x + (1 | site)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | region/site)",
    "d ~ a + x + (1 | region/site)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | block) + (1 | a:block)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | region/site) + (1 | a:region) + ...",
    "d ~ x + (1 + x | group)",
    "unbalanced random / nested / block"
  ),
  `Specialised implementation` = c(
    "permanova_unbalanced(); permanova_oneway() is the direct one-factor reference",
    "permanova_unbalanced()",
    "permanova_mixed()",
    "permanova_mixed_covariate()",
    "permanova_nested()",
    "permanova_nested_covariate()",
    "permanova_crossed()",
    "permanova_hybrid()",
    "permanova_random_slope_continuous()",
    "permanova_unequal_random_intercept() / permanova_unbalanced_*()"
  ),
  `Denominator or permutation` = c(
    "Within-group residual; unrestricted observations",
    "Full-model residual; term-specific Freedman-Lane",
    "Exact whole-plot EMS",
    "Split-plot or randomized-block covariate strata",
    "Level-specific EMS; descendants move intact",
    "Covariate-adjusted nested strata",
    "Exact a:block EMS; intact cells within block",
    "Exact a:region EMS; intact treatment profiles",
    "Between-group slope; whole-group sign flips",
    "Unit-centroid inference; size- or topology-restricted permutations"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(implementation)
```
`permanova_capabilities()` returns the complete machine-readable support table,
including estimands, error-control claims, and explicit exclusions.
